plain_title: When an object or cross-dressing brings distress
one_liner: Arousal from objects, body parts, or cross-dressing, diagnosed only when it causes real distress or problems.
in_simple_words: Fetishistic disorder involves intense arousal from non-living objects or from a specific non-genital body part. Transvestic disorder involves arousal from cross-dressing. Both are common as interests and harm no one, so neither is a disorder unless it causes real distress or problems, such as guilt, damaging secrecy, or needing it to the exclusion of everything else. Cross-dressing is not the same as being transgender. These diagnoses are rare, and therapy focuses on shame and relationships, not on removing the interest.
what_it_can_feel_like: My partner found out and we had the hardest conversation of our marriage. Couples therapy helped us both understand it. We're fine now.
I used to feel disgusted with myself after. The therapist asked who I was hurting. The answer was only me, with the shame.
common_signs: Recurring arousal from objects, non-genital body parts, or cross-dressing
Disorder only if causing distress, impairment, or relationship harm
Shame, secrecy, or conflict with a partner are usually the real problem

myths_vs_facts.myth: Having a fetish means something is wrong with you.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Fetishes are common and harmless. The DSM only calls it a disorder when it causes real distress or problems.

myths_vs_facts.myth: Men who cross-dress are gay or transgender.
myths_vs_facts.fact: Most people with transvestic interests are heterosexual men who identify as men. Gender identity, sexual orientation, and cross-dressing are three different things.

how_common.plain: Fetishistic and cross-dressing interests are common; the disorders, defined by distress, are rare and rarely diagnosed.
how_common.figure: Prevalence of the disorders not established; fetishism was among the most commonly reported interests in a Czech population study

what_helps.plain_summary: Therapy aims to reduce shame and distress, improve communication with partners, and help the person integrate the interest into a life and relationships they're happy with. Couples therapy often helps. Treating depression or anxiety matters. There's no good reason to try to eliminate a harmless interest, and attempts to do so tend to fail and increase distress.
evidence_based_options: Sex-positive or kink-aware psychotherapy for shame and distress
Treatment of co-occurring depression or anxiety
Psychoeducation for the person and partner
self_help_that_supports_care: Learning how common these interests are
Honest conversation with a partner at the right time, with support if needed
Noticing whether the distress is the interest or the secrecy
Finding a clinician who won't be shocked

when_to_reach_out: If an interest in objects or cross-dressing is causing you distress, guilt, or relationship problems, a sex-positive therapist can help. If you think your feelings about cross-dressing are about who you are rather than arousal, the gender dysphoria card may be more relevant.
is_not: Enjoying a fetish or cross-dressing without distress isn't a disorder. Being transgender or gender non-conforming is not transvestic disorder. Using objects designed for sex isn't fetishism.
hope_note: Most people find the problem was the shame, not the interest, and that shame can be set down.

content_notes: Strictly non-sensational: no descriptions of acts, no victim-blaming, no eroticised language.
Clear line between consensual adult interests (not a disorder) and non-consent or harm (always wrong, regardless of diagnosis).
